# Theme 6 Review

<!-- This file is the source of a page on the course website. Read it there: https://ai.buas.nl/open-courses/introduction-to-ml/self-study/theme-6/04_review.html -->

You have practiced communicating technical work, reading research and testing an idea from a paper. This page sums up the theme and checks the main ideas.

## Summary

- [Communicating Technical Work](01_communicating_technical_work.qmd): principles for presentations and for writing, turned into your own checklists. A document is useful when it is valuable to its reader.
- [Understanding ML Research](02_understanding_ml_research.qmd): types of research output, authorship and peer review, the scientific method, searching the literature, and why published results depend on the setting in which they were obtained.
- [Research to Practice](03_from_research_to_practice.qmd): choose a principle from a paper, apply it to a project, and evaluate the change under your usual validation.

## Quiz

These questions are easy if you have worked through the activities. Choose an answer to see whether it is right and why.

::: {.quiz data-answer="2"}
According to the lecture on writing, what matters most in a technical document?

- That it is complete and covers every detail. [A complete document can still be useless to its reader.]{.feedback}
- That it is valuable to the reader. [Right. Clear, organized and persuasive writing only helps if the content is valuable to the reader.]{.feedback}
- That it uses the technical terms of the field. [Terms help when the reader knows them, but they are not what makes a document useful.]{.feedback}
:::

::: {.quiz data-answer="1"}
You look for papers about a general method, such as hyperparameter optimization. How do you start?

- Broad searches first, then more specific ones. [Right. The broad searches give you the words for the specific ones.]{.feedback}
- By searching for the exact title of the best paper on the topic. [You usually do not know that title yet; finding it is the goal of the search.]{.feedback}
- By reading only the most cited paper. [Citations show attention, not that a paper fits your problem.]{.feedback}
:::

::: {.quiz data-answer="3"}
A highly cited paper reports that a technique improves results. What do you do before you rely on it?

- Nothing: many citations show that the technique works. [Results depend on the data, the models and the evaluation in the paper, as the SMOTE example shows.]{.feedback}
- Use it only if the paper is recent, because newer methods replace older ones. [Newer is not always better; what matters is whether it works in your setting.]{.feedback}
- Check its setting, and test it on your own problem. [Right. Collect your own evidence under your own validation.]{.feedback}
:::

::: {.quiz data-answer="1"}
You test an idea from a paper in your project. How do you evaluate it?

- Compare with and without the change on the same validation folds. [Right. Then a difference comes from the change, not from other folds.]{.feedback}
- Look at the test score after the change, because it is the most honest score. [Choosing on the test score makes it too optimistic.]{.feedback}
- Check whether the authors used the same dataset as you. [That is useful background, but it does not evaluate the change in your project.]{.feedback}
:::
